title: A New Flying Drone Uses Touch to Perch Like a Bird
summary:
A new flying robot can feel its way onto a branch and hang there like a bird. Its three human-like fingers grasp many shapes, letting the robot hang out in one spot.

Perching could let drones stay in one place, watching factories and power lines. Many drones use vision to perch, but in crowded spaces their view can be blocked. This design uses touch sensors instead, and once it grabs on, its three fingers hold tight with no extra energy. Researchers described the design August 22 in npj Robotics.

Anton Bredenbeck, a roboticist at Delft University of Technology, wanted a robot to study fragile ecosystems. 'The problem,' he says, 'is that drones are really, really inefficient flyers.' A drone could not fly nonstop for a month, so his team decided to attach their flyers to the world around them.

Birds inspired the idea: they use sight to spot a perch from far away, but touch guides the landing. The drone hangs below its perch, using fingers placed like a thumb, pointer finger, and middle finger. Each finger has three parts of different lengths, called phalanges. Touch sensors around soft silicone pads tell the drone when to close its fingers. Springs keep the fingers shut, like a clothespin's springs. A motor opens them by pulling metal cords that work like tendons.
why_it_matters: Drones that can perch like birds could one day help watch over nature and buildings near your home without flying around all the time.

keywords.explanation: Perching means landing on something and staying there, like a bird on a branch.
Phalanges are the small bone parts that make up a finger.
Silicone is a soft, bendy material a bit like rubber.
Tendons are strong cords in your body that pull on bones to move them.
A roboticist is a person who designs and builds robots.
Ecosystems are places where living things and nature all work together.

background_read: A drone is a flying robot, and this new one can perch, which means it can land on something and hang there in one place like a bird.
Instead of using sight to find a perch, it uses touch sensors, so it can grab on even where its view is blocked.
Perching lets a drone stay put to watch things like factories and power lines without wasting energy on flying, and the idea was inspired by how birds land.

WHAT: A new flying drone that uses touch to perch and hang in one place like a bird.
WHERE: On branches and other perches, where the drone hangs below and grips with its fingers.
WHY: To study fragile ecosystems and watch places like factories and power lines without wasting energy on flying.
